title: Interval tree — covered size
label: idb
statement:
Implement:

void addInterval(int start, int end)

Must be O(log n).

int getCoveredSize()

Must be O(1).

Use a segment tree or interval tree.

Discuss assumptions around: coordinate ranges, overlapping intervals, adjacent intervals, duplicates, removal if relevant.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Implement:
> 
> void addInterval(int start, int end)
> 
> Must be O(log n).
> 
> int getCoveredSize()
> 
> Must be O(1).
> 
> Use a segment tree or interval tree.
> 
> Discuss assumptions around: coordinate ranges, overlapping intervals, adjacent intervals, duplicates, removal if relevant.

A running total of covered ground. Intervals arrive one at a time, they overlap arbitrarily, and at any moment you must be able to say how much of the line is covered — counting overlapped regions once.

`getCoveredSize()` returns the total length of the union of everything added. Not the sum of the lengths — the length of the union.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Is the interval closed `[start, end]` or half-open `[start, end)`? It changes the answer to `getCoveredSize()` and it changes whether `[1,5]` and `[5,9]` merge.

I take **half-open**, so length is `end - start` and touching intervals coalesce. That is the convention that makes the arithmetic clean and matches how intervals are represented almost everywhere in practice. Under the closed reading, `[1,5]` has length 5 rather than 4, and `[1,5]` followed by `[6,9]` should merge because the integers are adjacent — which means the merge condition needs `prev.End + 1 >= start` instead of `prev.End >= start`.

This is not pedantry: it is one of the assumptions the statement explicitly asks you to discuss, and it is the difference between two implementations that both look right.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Half-open `[start, end)`; length is `end - start`. | Under the closed convention every length is one larger and the merge condition needs a +1. **This is the assumption to state first** — the statement asks about adjacent intervals precisely because of it. |
| `end <= start` is an empty interval and is ignored. | Alternatively throw. Ignoring is friendlier and makes the structure total; either way, say which, because a test will pass `(7,7)`. |
| No removal in the base problem. | The statement says "removal if relevant". Removal is genuinely harder: it can **split** one stored interval into two, so the interval count can grow on a remove, which breaks the amortised argument that makes insertion cheap. |
| Coordinates are arbitrary `int`, not a small bounded range. | This is what rules out a classic array-backed segment tree, which needs a bounded universe. It is the reason the answer is a sorted set of merged intervals rather than the structure the statement suggests — and explaining that choice is most of the value here. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Read the two constraints together and they tell you the design.

`getCoveredSize()` is **O(1)**. There is no structure over n intervals that can compute a union length in constant time on demand, so the answer cannot be computed at query time at all. It has to be **maintained as a field**, updated on every mutation. That is the first half, and it is the half people miss because it sounds too simple.

For the total to be maintainable, the stored intervals must be **disjoint and merged at all times** — an invariant, not a cleanup step. If overlapping intervals could sit in the structure, the union length would not be the sum of their lengths and the running total would be meaningless. So `addInterval` does the merging, and `getCoveredSize` becomes `return _covered;`.

Now, `addInterval` in O(log n). The new interval merges with its immediate predecessor if that one reaches it, and swallows every interval starting inside its extended span. Finding the predecessor is a search, not a scan, which is where the log comes from. Each swallowed interval is subtracted from the total as it is removed, and the merged result is added once.

And here is the part worth being precise about: **a single insert can remove many intervals, so one call is not O(log n)**. It is O(k log n) for k absorbed. But each interval can only ever be removed once, so across any sequence of m inserts the total removal work is bounded by m — the cost is **amortised** O(log n). That is the honest statement of the bound, and the adversarial input that proves the worst case is one line: insert a thousand tiny disjoint intervals, then one huge one.

Finally, why not the structure the statement suggests. A classic array-backed **segment tree needs a bounded coordinate universe** — you size the array to the coordinate range. With arbitrary `int` coordinates that is four billion slots. The fixes are coordinate compression (which needs all the intervals up front, and they arrive one at a time) or a dynamic, lazily-allocated segment tree (which works and is much more code for the same asymptotics). A sorted set of merged intervals is the right answer here, and being able to say **why** the suggested structure does not fit is better than using it because it was suggested.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Keep every interval in a list as given. On `getCoveredSize()`, sort by start, sweep, merge on the fly and sum. *`addInterval` O(1), `getCoveredSize` O(n log n). Space O(n).*

**Why not good enough.** It violates the one constraint the question is built on, and it does so in the expensive direction: queries are usually far more frequent than inserts for a structure like this. The fix is to move the work from the query to the insert — which is the general shape of every "maintain an aggregate" problem, and worth naming as such. A middle option, caching the total and invalidating on insert, is worse than both: it is O(n log n) on the first query after any insert, so a read-write-read pattern gets the bad case every time.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `AddInterval(int start, int end)`, arriving one at a time |
| TRANSFORMATION | The new interval is merged with every interval it touches, producing one wider interval |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `SortedSet<(int Start, int End)>` holding **disjoint, merged** intervals, plus a `long _covered` running total |
| ALGORITHM | Find the predecessor via `GetViewBetween`; absorb it if it reaches the new start; then repeatedly absorb the lowest interval starting inside the span; insert the result and adjust the total |
| OUTPUT | `GetCoveredSize()` returns the field |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `end <= start` → return; nothing to cover.
- Set `lo = start`, `hi = end`.
- Find the last interval with `Start <= start`. If its `End >= start`, it reaches the new interval: extend `lo` and `hi` to cover it, and drop it.
- Loop: find the lowest interval with `Start` in `[lo, hi]`. If none, stop. Otherwise extend `hi` to cover it and drop it.
- Insert `(lo, hi)` and add its length to the total.
- `Drop` both removes from the set **and** subtracts from the total, so the two can never disagree.

- `getCoveredSize()` must be **O(1)**. That single requirement is what forces the design: the answer cannot be computed on demand, so it must be maintained.
- `addInterval` must be O(log n), which means finding where the interval belongs by search rather than by scan.
- Intervals may overlap, nest, touch, or duplicate. All four have to be handled and they are not the same case.
- Coordinates are `int`, so the total can exceed `int.MaxValue` and must accumulate in a `long`.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `SortedSet<(int, int)>` rather than `SortedList` or `SortedDictionary` | `SortedList` is array-backed, so insertion is O(n) from the memmove — it looks right and breaks the bound. `SortedDictionary` is a red-black tree with O(log n) insert but **no predecessor query**, which is the one operation needed. `SortedSet.GetViewBetween` is O(log n) and gives both `Min` and `Max` of a range, so it is the only one of the three that fits. This is a genuinely C#-specific piece of knowledge and worth stating as the reason. |
| Sorting on the tuple, which orders by `Start` then `End` | Safe **because the intervals are disjoint** — for disjoint intervals, ordering by start is the same as ordering by end, so the default tuple comparer cannot produce a wrong order. That is a consequence of the invariant, not a coincidence, and it is why no custom comparer is needed. |
| A `long _covered` field | The entire reason `getCoveredSize` is O(1). `long` because `int` coordinates can sum past `int.MaxValue`. |
| Merged intervals as an invariant | Not a tidy-up. The total is only meaningful if the stored intervals are disjoint, so the invariant is what the O(1) query rests on. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`GetViewBetween` is the whole reason this is `SortedSet`.** `GetViewBetween((int.MinValue, int.MinValue), (start, int.MaxValue)).Max` is "the last interval starting at or before `start`" — a predecessor query, in O(log n). `SortedDictionary` cannot do this at all, and `SortedList` can via `BinarySearch` but then pays O(n) on insert. The choice of collection is the technical content of this question in C#.

**Why the absorb loop re-creates the view each iteration.** Absorbing an interval can push `hi` further right, which brings intervals into range that were previously outside it. The view is a **range query**, so it has to be re-taken after `hi` changes. Taking it once and enumerating would miss the cascade — and would also mutate the set while enumerating a view of it, which throws.

**`Drop` does both jobs, deliberately.** It removes from the set and subtracts from `_covered` in one place. The invariant "`_covered` equals the sum of the stored lengths" then cannot drift, because there is exactly one path that removes an interval. Separate remove and subtract calls would give two places for them to disagree, and the resulting bug is a silently wrong total with a perfectly correct set.

**Why the default tuple comparer is safe.** Sorting `(Start, End)` compares `End` only when two intervals share a `Start`, which cannot happen while the set is disjoint. So the comparer never sees the ambiguous case. This follows from the invariant rather than from luck, and if the invariant were ever broken the ordering would break too — which is a good argument for the invariant being maintained by one method rather than by convention.

**`prev.End >= start`, not `>`.** Under the half-open convention, `[1,5)` and `[5,9)` are adjacent with no gap, so they should merge into `[1,9)`. `>=` merges them; `>` leaves two intervals that happen to touch. Both give the same **covered total**, but the second lets the interval count grow without bound on adjacent inserts, which slowly destroys the search performance. The total being right either way is what makes this bug hard to notice.

**`long _covered`.** Two `int` coordinates can span more than `int.MaxValue`, and summing several such spans certainly can. `int` would overflow silently to a negative total.

**`Snapshot()` exists for the tests.** It lets the test assert that the stored set really is disjoint and sorted after 300 random trials, not just that the total is right. A correct total with a corrupt set is a bug waiting for the next insert, so both are checked.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GetCoveredSize` | O(1) | O(1) | Returns a field. This is the requirement, met literally. |
| `AddInterval` | O(log n) **amortised** | O(1) | One predecessor query plus k removals, each O(log n); k is amortised O(1) |
| `AddInterval` worst case | O(k log n) | O(1) | A single interval spanning k stored intervals absorbs all k |
| space | — | O(n) | n is the number of **merged** intervals, which can be far below the number added |

**The amortised argument is the answer to the question, not a footnote.** Each interval is inserted once and removed at most once, so over m inserts the total removal work is O(m log n) and the per-operation average is O(log n). The worst single call is unbounded in k, and the adversarial input is trivial: insert [0,1), [2,3), [4,5) … 1,000 times, then insert [0,2000). That one call removes 1,000 intervals. Stating the bound as strict O(log n) is wrong; stating it as amortised **and producing the counterexample** is the strongest available answer, because the statement asked for something that cannot be delivered literally.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty structure | `GetCoveredSize()` returns 0. |
| `end <= start` | Ignored. `(7,7)` and `(9,3)` both change nothing. |
| Fully contained interval | Absorbed by the predecessor; the total does not change. |
| Exact duplicate | Same as contained — no change. |
| Adjacent, `[1,5)` then `[5,9)` | Merges to `[1,9)` under the half-open reading. Under the closed reading `[1,5]` and `[6,9]` should also merge, needing `+1` in the condition. |
| Bridging interval | Absorbs the predecessor and every interval it reaches, cascading. The walkthrough case. |
| Negative coordinates | Work. `int.MinValue` sentinels in the view bound mean the predecessor query still finds them. |
| `int.MinValue` / `int.MaxValue` as real coordinates | The sentinel bounds collide with genuine data at the extremes. If those values are legal, the view bounds need to be `long`-typed or the comparer needs a sentinel flag. Worth stating; unlikely to be tested; wrong to claim it is handled. |
| Total exceeding `int.MaxValue` | Accumulated in a `long`. |
| Many adjacent inserts | Coalesce, so the interval count stays low and the search stays fast. This is the payoff for using `>=` rather than `>`. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Support removeInterval. What breaks?**

Find every stored interval overlapping the removed range. For each: subtract its length from the total, remove it, then re-insert whatever survives — the part to the left of the removed range, the part to the right, or both. Removing `[4,6)` from `[1,10)` leaves `[1,4)` and `[6,10)`, so **one interval became two**.

*Trade-off:* Two things break. The interval count can now grow on a removal, so the set can be larger than the number of inserts — memory is no longer bounded by insert count. And the amortised argument for insertion weakens: intervals can be created by removals, so "each interval is removed at most once" no longer bounds the work by the number of `AddInterval` calls. The bound becomes amortised in the total number of **operations** rather than inserts. The O(1) query survives untouched, which is the good news. **This is LeetCode 715 Range Module, and it is rated Hard** — which is the honest difficulty for the pair.

**Why not the segment tree you were told to use?**

A classic segment tree is an array sized to the **coordinate universe**. With arbitrary `int` coordinates that is 2³² leaves, which is not allocatable. Two fixes exist. **Coordinate compression** maps the coordinates that actually appear onto a small range — but it needs all the intervals up front, and here they arrive one at a time, so it does not apply. A **dynamic segment tree** allocates nodes lazily as coordinates are touched, which does work: O(log C) per operation for coordinate range C, with a covered count maintained at the root.

A segment tree becomes the better answer when the queries get richer — "how much is covered between x and y" rather than "how much in total" — because that is a range query the sorted set cannot answer in logarithmic time.

*Trade-off:* The sorted set is far less code, has space proportional to the number of merged intervals rather than to the coordinate range, and meets both stated bounds. The dynamic segment tree buys range queries and lazy propagation, and costs substantially more code and O(log C) with a larger constant. **I would build the sorted set and say exactly this** — including that I would switch if range queries were added.

**What about the coordinate range, and negative coordinates?**

The sorted set is agnostic: coordinates are only ever compared, never used as indices, so negatives and the full `int` range work with no special handling. The one genuine wrinkle is that `int.MinValue` and `int.MaxValue` are used as sentinels in the `GetViewBetween` bounds, so if those exact values can be real coordinates the bounds need widening to `long` or the comparer needs a sentinel flag.

*Trade-off:* This agnosticism is precisely the advantage over the array-backed segment tree, whose size is the coordinate range. It is the strongest argument for the choice and it follows directly from an assumption the statement asked about — so it is worth connecting the two out loud.

**Make it thread-safe.**

A `ReaderWriterLockSlim` fits the access pattern: `GetCoveredSize` is a read and `AddInterval` is a write, and reads are expected to dominate. Reads are then concurrent and writes are exclusive.

There is a cheaper option specifically because the query is a single field: compute the new total into a local during the insert and publish it **once** with a single `Volatile.Write`, so a reader taking no lock at all sees either the old value or the new one and never an intermediate. That makes `GetCoveredSize` truly lock-free.

*Trade-off:* `ReaderWriterLockSlim` is simple and obviously correct, and it has real acquisition cost on a read-heavy path. The single-publish trick makes reads free and requires care that no intermediate value is ever written to the field — which means restructuring `Drop` so it accumulates into a local rather than mutating the field as it goes. I would start with the lock and only do the second if the read path were measured as hot.

**Also answer "is point p covered?" and "how much is covered in [x, y)?"**

**Is p covered** is O(log n) on the existing set: find the predecessor of p and test whether its end passes p. Nothing else needed.

**How much is covered in [x, y)** cannot be done in logarithmic time by this structure — it needs the sum of clipped lengths over a range, which is O(k) in the intervals inside it. To get O(log n) you need an order-statistic tree augmented with subtree length sums, or the dynamic segment tree from the earlier follow-up, where the sum is already maintained per node.

*Trade-off:* **This is the requirement that would make me switch structures**, and that is the point worth making: the sorted set is the right answer to the question as asked, and the wrong answer to a slightly richer one. Naming the condition under which you would change your mind is more useful than defending the first choice.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and space complexity? Can it be improved? What happens as N grows?* — States both, names the bottleneck
